headline: New moon springs stack the tide at Plum Gut as bass and porgies both show
subhead: Bigger water builds toward the July 11-13 peak, fluke get shoved out of the warm bay into Mattituck's mouth, and the Gut starts working again on the push.
body_markdown:
Sixty years on this shoreline and I still pay attention to the moon before I pay attention to the weatherman. We're running down toward new moon, and you can feel it in the current already — the tide's been building each day this week, bigger swing morning and night, and by the weekend we'll be into full spring tides. That matters more here than almost anywhere else on the Island, because my water lives and dies on current. Plum Gut and the Race don't fish on slack. They fish on push. Last week was mixed — we had some blow come through mid-week that roiled things up along Horton Point and Rocky Point, dropped visibility to soup for a day or two, and the fish scattered off the structure until it settled. By Sunday it had cleaned back up and the current started doing what current does — stacking bait against the rocks.

This week the tides keep building right through the new moon, with the biggest exchanges lining up Friday through Monday. That's not just a Sound Shore thing — I'm hearing the western end of the Sound is set up the same way, with the evening flood converging right on sunset for the first time since the June full moon. Out here it means the same thing: moving water late in the day, right as the light goes gold, right when the bass want to work. If you've got one window to fish this week, that's the one I'd take — the last two hours of the incoming, running into dusk, anywhere current stacks against structure. Horton Point's boulder field, the rip off Rocky Point, and the top of the Gut approach where the reef breaks the flow — those are the three places I'd put a boat or a set of waders.

Fluke have been the more reliable story the last ten days, and it's not really a Sound Shore pattern so much as a squeeze. The bay's been running warm — warm enough that the fluke that usually spread out over the flats have bailed for cooler, cleaner water, and that means they're stacking at the mouths where bay water meets Sound water. Mattituck Inlet has been the beneficiary. Fish are holding right where the outgoing current dumps warm water into cooler Sound water, and there's a temperature seam you can practically see as a color change on a calm morning. Four to five pound fluke have come out of that seam on the last two hours of the outgoing, fished with three-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on half-ounce bucktails, dragged dead slow along bottom. Don't work it fast — these fish are sitting in a comfort zone, not chasing. Let the bait do the work.

Bass have been spotty, and I'll say that plain instead of dressing it up. Guys working Plum Gut on the last two weeks have had good days and dead days, and the difference has almost always come down to current strength. When the tide's weak, the fish sit deep and sulk. When it's ripping — and it's about to start ripping harder as we build toward the new moon — they come up on the reef edges and feed hard for a short window. Eels have been the go-to there, drifted or slow-trolled through the Gut on the last of the ebb, and bucktails tipped with a strip of squid have worked the same water when the current's too strong to hold an eel straight. Bluefish have been mixed in with the bass at the Gut, not thick, but present enough that if you're fishing bait you'll get bit by something with teeth sooner or later. Nothing wrong with that this time of year — a few slammers in the 4-6 pound range have come through on diamond jigs worked fast through the rip.

Porgies are the one thing out here that hasn't let anybody down. Structure fishing off Rocky Point and the rock piles east of Horton Point has been steady — not spectacular, but steady, which for porgies is exactly what you want. Squid strips and clam on a hi-lo rig, bottom fished right on the rocks, and you'll fill a bucket most mornings. Blackfish have started showing on the same structure as water settles, though it's early for them yet — a few keepers to three pounds on green crab, nothing to build a trip around but worth a rod in the spread if you're anchored up for porgies anyway.

Weakfish I'll mention only because people keep asking. They're just not here in numbers worth chasing. Water's been plenty warm enough for a while now, and the fish haven't followed the temperature the way the books say they should. I wouldn't burn a tide targeting them — if one shows up mixed in with the bass at the Gut, treat it like a bonus, not a plan.

Looking ahead, I'm watching Friday through Monday close. If the wind stays out of the south and lays down at night the way it's been trending, that sunset flood at the Gut and off Horton Point should be the best current-and-light combination we've had since spring. I'd fish the last two hours of the incoming into dark, eels or bucktails at the Gut, bucktails and Gulp at Mattituck's mouth on the fluke. If the wind kicks up out of the northeast instead, I'd shift inside to the porgy grounds and wait the blow out — that bite doesn't care much what the sky's doing.
